The herald, briefly

I have been asked to describe the furniture

Last time I sold you the idea. This time I am handing you the inventory — every wall you will break, every man who will object, and every heavy golden thing you will drop on a staircase.

Each sheet below is drawn against one rule: a standard man is 1.80 metres, and nothing that guards a room may be taller than that room. Rooms sit on a twelve-metre cell. Gold is orpiment and only orpiment; verdigris is only ever something you may touch; the voice alone is lapis. The full build notes for each thing — sizes, materials, rigs, how it breaks — are in the handoff sheet it links to.

The measure

1.80 m standard human. Clear heights: Crypt 3.00 · Outer Bailey 3.60 · Inner Ward 4.00 · Keep 4.60 · Curtain Wall open. Archways 2.60 m wide.

The household

Men and animals only — no spirits, no constructs. Four to an Age: the patrol, the ranged, the heavy, and the one the century is remembered for.

The plunder

Worth in coin, bulk in stone, fragility in the speed that ruins it. Over ten stone takes two of you. These are the numbers the game's loot assets carry.

Stratum I · c. 1200 BC
c. 1200 BCStratum I
The Bronze Age

Citadels of mud-brick and smoke

Behold the oldest door in the lair, and the lowest ceiling. Here are citadels of painted plaster and mud-brick piled on stones so vast the later Greeks swore giants set them; here are grain stores, oil stores, and kings who are also gods and will say so at length, by firelight, through a haze of their own hearth-smoke. The household is many, and bravely dressed in linen, and has never in its life seen a crossbow bolt — which you may consider either a mercy or an opportunity. One warning, and I give it freely: everything in this century is dry. The rafters are dry, the oil is dry-stored, the priests carry fire about on poles. Say IGNIS here and mean it modestly.

The stonework

Three pieces of building. Each sits on the twelve-metre cell and knows its own joins.

The Bronze Age · CurtainWall
The Lion Gate
A cyclopean gateway under a corbelled triangle and two carved lions, closing on timber doors.

The way in, and the citadel's opinion of you, carved in the same stone. Two stretches of cyclopean masonry — blocks so large the later Greeks credited them to one-eyed giants — pinch a passage down to a single pair of timber doors under a lintel of twenty tonnes. Above it the builders left a corbelled triangle to spare the lintel, and filled it with a relief of two lions at a column, which is a king explaining that he owns both the gate and the lions. The doors bar from inside and burn from outside; the walls do neither, and the gate is the only thing in this Age that shrugs at FRANGO.

Footprint: 12 × 12 m, one cell; gate passage runs north–south through the middle · Height: 5.20 m
Sockets: Door (gate), N–S through the cell centre: 2.60 × 3.74 m clear (CurtainWall archway), double timber leaves, barred from the north side · Stair: east mass, inner (north) face — 1.00 m wide stone stair of 14 risers (0.293 m) rising west-to-east to the wall-walk at 4.10 m · Arrow-loop (sling slots): 3 per parapet, 0.12 × 0.50 m, splayed to 0.40 m inside, centred 0.60 m above the wall-walk (4.70 m) · Murder-hole: none — Bronze Age gates are defended from the flanking masses, not overhead; the wall-walks are open for slingers · Torch sockets: 2 bronze ring brackets on the north face, 2.20 m up, 0.30 m either side of the passage
In play: The doors are the weak point: IGNIS sets the timber leaves burning in 6 s and they fall off their pivots at 20 s; FRANGO splits the bar (not the stone). · The cyclopean masses are indestructible — the only structure in the Age FRANGO cannot touch; it chips a chinking stone loose for show. · Wall-walk slingers at 4.10 m cover the approach from behind the parapet; the relief triangle has no walk over it, so junk thrown up from the gate passage lands on the walk behind. · The cart-wheel ruts are a physics bump: a two-carrier load dragged through the gate bounces and may drop. · The lion slab can be pried out with 3 FRANGO hits and falls inward as a 1.6 t crushing prop (kills anything under it).

The Bronze Age · Keep
The Megaron
The king's hall: a painted circular hearth, four columns, a throne, and a hole in the roof for the smoke to find its own way out.

Here is where a god-king sits to be warm and important. A great round hearth fills the middle of the floor, painted in rings of flame and running spiral; four red-painted columns of cypress hold up a roof of reed and clay, with a lantern-hole above the fire where the smoke leaves, eventually. The walls are frescoed with griffins, processions and the king's opinion of himself; the throne is plastered into the east wall so nobody can steal it, which is a challenge. Low, warm, soot-darkened and full of things that burn: the finest room in the Age and the easiest to lose.

Footprint: 12 × 12 m, one cell; hall 10.4 × 8.8 m inside, 1.6 m porch on the south · Height: 4.60 m
Sockets: Door, south face (main, through the porch): 2.60 × 3.31 m (Keep archway), timber double leaves on pivots · Door, north face: 2.60 × 3.31 m archway, hung with a heavy wool curtain rather than doors (burns in 3 s) · Door, west face: 2.60 × 3.31 m archway to the store rooms · East face: no door — the throne wall; the archway rule is satisfied by a blind 2.60 × 3.31 m recess behind the throne holding a secret niche (1.00 × 0.60 × 1.20 m) · Window: 2 clerestory slots, north and south walls, 1.20 × 0.40 m at 3.90 m (light and smoke only, not climbable) · Smoke-hole: 2.00 × 2.00 m roof opening over the hearth — a vertical socket to the roof tile above
In play: Fire hazard: the hearth is always lit (point light, flicker 0.2 Hz); IGNIS anywhere in the room spreads to the ceiling beams within 8 s and the whole roof underside burns in 30 s — then smoke fills from the top down, 0.10 m/s. · The four columns are FRANGO-breakable (3 hits each); lose two on one side and that roof quarter drops, blocking an archway with burning debris. · The throne's secret niche holds the Age's artifact spawn (gold death-mask or faience); prying it is loud (alerts the hall). · The wool curtain on the north archway blocks line of sight but not bodies; set it alight to cut off pursuit for 12 s. · Low for a Keep and full of smoke once burning: thrown loot arcs clip the 4.60 m beams.

The Bronze Age · InnerWard
The Pithos Magazine
Rows of man-high storage jars — grain on one side, olive oil on the other — and aisles too narrow to turn in.

The wealth of the palace in its plainest form: grain and oil, by the tonne, in jars taller than you are. The pithoi stand set into clay benches in four rows, each one tattooed with rope-pattern bands and a scribe's mark of what it holds and whose it is. The aisles are narrow enough that a man with a tower shield must walk them sideways. Grain burns. Oil burns better. A lit fire-pot through that door turns the magazine into the brightest room in the century for a good eleven minutes.

Footprint: 12 × 12 m, one cell; four rows of jars N–S with five aisles, one E–W cross-aisle · Height: 4.00 m
Sockets: Door, south face: 2.60 × 2.88 m (InnerWard archway), single timber leaf, often propped · Door, north face: 2.60 × 2.88 m archway into the next magazine · Door, east and west faces: 2.60 × 2.88 m archways opening onto the wall aisles; each is half-choked by a stacked amphora pile 0.60 m inside it that must be broken or climbed · Window: 2 vent holes in the ceiling, 0.60 × 0.60 m (smoke escape; not climbable) · Stair: none — the magazine is a ground-floor room · Hide spots: 8 marked crouch spots where the cross-aisle meets each row end (jar bellies nearly touch along a row at 1.17 m pitch, so the only cover is at row ends and the cross-aisle)
In play: Conflagration: IGNIS on any oil pithos or pool ignites the whole east half in 4 s (burning oil flows downhill along the aisles at 0.6 m/s); the grain rows follow in 15 s; fire lasts ~11 min unless the roof falls in. · Pithoi are FRANGO-breakable (1 hit): grain jars spill a drift that slows movement 30%; oil jars spill a slick that makes everyone slip on a sprint and is flammable. · Aisles 1.20 m (0.90 m at clamps) force single file: a Dendra Champion must shuffle sideways and cannot swing his rapier in them — the room is where you fight him. · Crouch-hides between jars break line of sight; the Keeper of the Flame patrols here and a missed fire-pot is the most likely way the magazine goes up. · Loot spawns: sealed amphorae stacked at the south bench; oxhide ingots stored in a jar pit under the scribe's bench.

The household

Four defenders: the one who walks the walls, the one who shoots, the one you avoid, and the one this century is remembered for.

The Bronze Age · CurtainWall, OuterBailey
Palace Levypatrol
A farmer the king has lent a spear to: linen, a leather cap and a shield the size of a door.

Consider the palace levy: last week a man who kept goats, this week the first line of a god-king's defences, and in both roles chiefly concerned with his supper. He carries a figure-of-eight oxhide shield that covers him from chin to shin and a thrusting spear nearly half again his height, and he wears a linen tunic and a leather cap and that is all the armour the treasury would stand. There are a great many of him. He is slow to believe you are real, quick to shout once he does, and a crossbow bolt goes through him, his shield and the man behind.

Silhouette. A huge figure-of-eight shield like a pinched hourglass hiding the whole left side, a tall vertical spear line rising 0.7 m over the head, and a small round-capped head on a thin, bare-armed body.

The Bronze Age · CurtainWall, InnerWard
Wall Slingerranged
A lightly-dressed youth with a sling and a pouch of river stones; silent, quick, and unkind to helmets.

The slinger is the Bronze Age's answer to the question 'what if a rock, but faster'. He wears a kilt and a stone-pouch and very little else, and he stands on the wall with a cord in his hand and a lead-shaped stone in the cord, and the first you know of him is a sound like a slammed door on the side of your head. Light, quick, poorly paid and extremely accurate; he will not come down off the wall to meet you, and he runs the moment you arrive where he is.

Silhouette. A slim bare-chested figure with a long cord and cradle whirling over one shoulder in a loop, a bulging pouch on the hip, a bandana with two tails at the back of the head, and bare legs under a short wrapped kilt.

The Bronze Age · Keep, InnerWard
Dendra Championheavy
A nobleman sealed in a bronze bell of plates, a boar's-tusk helmet and a rapier as long as your arm and his.

The king's own champion, bolted into the Dendra panoply: fifteen pieces of hammered bronze in nested rings about his chest and hips, a neck-guard to his ears and a helmet of boar's tusk that took forty boars and one very patient man. He moves like a bell being carried downstairs and he cannot turn quickly, sit, or climb a ladder; but thrown pots and furniture bounce off him like rain off a shield, and his rapier reaches a remarkably long way. Fight him in a narrow place. Better still, fetch something from a later century with a point on it.

Silhouette. A stack of wide, flaring horizontal bronze bands — a cone on a bell — with huge rounded shoulder-guards, a tall neck collar hiding the chin, a conical helmet striped in pale tusk rows with a tuft on top, and a very long thin sword held low.

The Bronze Age · Keep, InnerWard, Crypt
Keeper of the Flamespecial
A temple priestess who carries the palace fire on a yoke of clay pots and throws it at you.

The keeper tends the god's fire, which in this Age means she carries it about in clay pots slung from a yoke across her shoulders, with a swinging brazier in her other hand for the incense and for emphasis. She is the only person in the palace who is entirely unafraid of you, having been raised to believe she is the fire's servant and you are merely its fuel. When alarmed she unhooks a pot and throws it; it breaks, it spills, it burns, and in a century built of dry timber and oil jars that is the end of the argument. Kill her far from anything you mean to keep.

Silhouette. A tall flounced tiered skirt like a stepped bell, a horizontal yoke across both shoulders with two round pots swinging from each end on cords, glowing orange pot-mouths, a high flat-topped headdress, and a censer on a chain in one hand.

The plunder

Five things worth the trip. Worth is coin at the lair; bulk is stone in your arms; the red bar is how little it takes to ruin it.

The Bronze Age · one carrier
Oxhide Ingot
A slab of Cypriot copper shaped like a flayed ox-skin, with four handles for corners.

Here is money before anyone thought of coin: a slab of pure copper, cast in the shape of a stretched ox-hide so a man may carry it on his shoulder by its four horned corners. It weighs about what a small child weighs and is roughly as easy to break as a promise made to a smith. It will not shatter, it will not dent, and if you throw it at a levy he will go down and it will not notice. Merchants of three empires will take it; so will we.

The Bronze Age · one carrier
Sealed Amphora
A Canaanite wine jar with a clay seal still on its mouth and the king's mark in the clay.

Wine, from somewhere with better grapes than here, in a jar shaped to be packed in the hold of a ship and to be carried by two handles and no dignity. The mouth is stoppered and sealed with a lump of clay pressed with a signet, which is how a king says 'this is mine' in a century without locks. It sloshes. Carry it level. Should you drop it, you will lose the wine, the worth, and your footing, in that order.

The Bronze Age · one carrier
Faience Hippopotamus
A small blue glazed hippopotamus from Egypt, painted with river plants and worth a great deal more than a real one.

An Egyptian gift to a king who has never seen a hippopotamus and so has no idea how badly they behave. It is small, bright blue, glazed like a wet river stone, painted all over with lotus flowers and marsh reeds in black, and it is precisely as fragile as it looks. Hold it in one hand; hold it close; do not, under any circumstances, run down a staircase with it. It is the most valuable thing per pound in the Age.

The Bronze Age · one carrier · artifact
Gold Death-Mask
A king's face beaten from a single sheet of gold, eyes shut, moustache twirled, laid over him for eternity until you arrived.

Some ancestor of the house, too grand to be allowed to rot in an ordinary face, was buried under this: a sheet of gold hammered over a wooden form into his likeness, eyes closed, beard combed, moustache upturned with the confidence of a man who never paid for anything. It is the single most valuable object in the Age and — I note with enthusiasm — it is light. It will not shatter; it crumples. Drop it hard and the old king's face folds in two and so does its price.

The Bronze Age · two carriers
Tripod Cauldron
A ceremonial bronze cauldron on three tall legs, ring-handled, heavy enough to need two of you and loud enough to wake everyone.

This is the kind of prize kings gave to other kings, and to heroes, and to gods, and — in one unfortunate instance — as a bribe to the sea. It is a deep bronze cauldron on three cast legs with two great ring handles, and it weighs rather more than a man. It takes two of you. It does not break; it dents, and every dent rings like a temple bell, so you may as well sing while you carry it.

Stratum II · c. 1250
c. 1250Stratum II
The High Medieval

Stone keeps and reliquaries

My own century, and the one you will learn on — so mind it. Curtain walls of honest limestone, spiral stairs that turn clockwise (not in your favour), and a chapel worth more than everything around it put together. The garrison is small and well-dressed in steel; the household wakes by degrees, a lantern here, a hound there, a knight last of all — which is precisely the order in which you will come to regret waking them.

The stonework

Three pieces of building. Each sits on the twelve-metre cell and knows its own joins.

The High Medieval · CurtainWall
The Gatehouse
Twin-towered gate passage with a portcullis, murder-holes in the vault and a barred pair of doors.

Here is the castle's one front door, and it has been designed by a man who assumed you would be rude enough to use it. Two D-shaped towers crowd a vaulted passage; a portcullis waits in its groove, three murder-holes squint down from the vault, and a pair of oak doors take a drawbar the size of a felled tree. It is also your way home: the extraction exit sits in this cell, so every raid ends by walking back under that portcullis and trusting nobody upstairs says TONITRUS.

Footprint: 12 × 12 m, one cell; block 9.0 × 10.0 m with two D-towers, curtain stubs east and west · Height: 5.20 m
Sockets: Door (archway), north face: 2.60 × 3.31 m, centred x 6.0 — the way in and the way home · Door (archway), south face: 2.60 × 3.31 m, centred x 6.0 — onto the bailey · Arrow-loop ×2, north tower faces: 0.10 × 1.10 m slit, sill 1.1 m, cross-oillet 0.40 m · Arrow-loop ×2, into the passage from each guard room at y 3.3 m: 0.10 × 1.10 m · Murder-hole ×3 in the vault at y 3.0 / 4.2 / 5.4 m: 0.30 × 0.30 m · Portcullis slot in the vault at y 1.2 m: 2.60 × 0.20 m · Stair (up), east tower: newel stair to the 4.60 m deck · Wall-walk ×2 at 4.60 m, east and west: 2.40 m wide, joining the curtain modules
In play: TONITRUS at the windlass (or FRANGO on its rope) drops the portcullis: 0.9 t falling 2 m, lethal to anything under it, and it seals the extraction path until LEVO or a crew hauls it back. · Murder-holes are sight-lines and pour points: guards on the deck drop boiling oil once the house is up (3 s warning hiss, madder splash decal). · The drawbar can be LEVO-lifted quietly or FRANGO-split loudly; once barred, the inner doors need 12 st of shove to force. · The torch is the only light in the passage: IGNIS on the doors burns them in 20 s; TONITRUS's fumble puts the torch out. · Guard rooms hide one Castle Crossbowman each behind the passage arrow-loops.
Full handoff sheet →
The High Medieval · Keep
The Newel Stair
A clockwise newel stair in a stone drum, linking one floor to the next — built for a right-handed defender coming down.

Behold the stair that turns clockwise, as every good castle stair does, so that the man above has his sword arm free and you have yours jammed against a pillar. It is a stone drum in the corner of a lobby, twenty-six worn treads around a single newel, with slits for light and a rope for your hand. It links one floor to the next, and it is where the altarpiece will be dropped, because it is always dropped on the stairs.

Footprint: 12 × 12 m, one cell; stair drum Ø 4.0 m outside / 2.4 m inside in the north-east corner, lobby room around it · Height: 4.60 m
Sockets: Stair-down: bottom doorway 0.90 × 2.10 m at floor level (0.30 m) — connects the stair from the floor below · Stair-up: top landing at +4.90 m, 0.90 m wide — onto the next floor's module · Door (archway) ×4, lobby, centred on each face: 2.60 × 3.31 m · Slit window ×3 in the drum: 0.10 × 0.90 m outside · Door, drum: 0.90 × 2.10 m oak leaf (lockable)
In play: Anything dropped on the stair rolls to the bottom and takes impact every tread: the Gilded Altarpiece arrives worth 0, the Silver Ewer arrives dented. · Two players carrying a dual-carry item must go single-file: the inner (newel) carrier moves at 60 % speed on the 0.03 m going. · Enemies coming down fight at full reach; players going up take a −20 % swing arc (the newel is in the way) — the pitch's clockwise joke, made mechanical. · The slits are too narrow to leave by; the rope rail can be burned (IGNIS), after which a TONITRUS on the stair knocks a player down the helix.

The High Medieval · Keep
The Chapel
A small two-bay vaulted chapel with a painted altar, a gilded retable and five stained-glass lancets.

Here, friends, is where the money is kept, though the priest would call it something else. A two-bay rib-vaulted room of limewashed stone, an altar dressed in red, the gilded retable on top, candles either side, and five windows of coloured glass that will announce your visit to the entire household the moment anything is thrown near them. It is the richest room in the Age, and the most fragile.

Footprint: 12 × 12 m, one cell; nave 8.4 × 5.4 m inside, sacristy strip to the north · Height: 4.60 m
Sockets: Door (archway), west: 2.60 × 3.31 m into the nave — the main way in · Door (archway), north and south of the cell: 2.60 × 3.31 m (north into the sacristy strip, south into the side passage) · Door (archway), east of the cell: 2.60 × 3.31 m, opens into the passage behind the altar wall, not the nave · Window ×5 (stained-glass lancets): 3 east 0.45–0.50 × 2.10–2.40 m, 2 south 0.45 × 2.10 m, sill 1.80 m · Door, sacristy: 0.90 × 2.10 m · Prop socket: retable on the mensa (Gilded Altarpiece), 2 candle stands, altar plate on the mensa front
In play: Each lancet shatters at 2 m/s impact (a thrown ewer does it) — the loudest single noise in the Age, waking every guard within two cells. · The retable is the Gilded Altarpiece: taking it off the mensa is silent; dropping it on the step is not. · IGNIS burns the frontal cloth and benches (candles make it easy to do by accident); the stone vault does not burn. · AURUM VOCO lights the whole east end — the altarpiece, the plate, the reliquary in the sacristy chest. · The one Household Knight posted in the Keep stands his watch here.

The household

Four defenders: the one who walks the walls, the one who shoots, the one you avoid, and the one this century is remembered for.

The High Medieval · CurtainWall, OuterBailey
Lantern Wardenpatrol
The night watch: a quilted man with a horn lantern and a glaive, walking a fixed round.

The humblest man in the household and the most useful, for he carries the only light on the walls. A padded wool coat, an iron kettle hat, a glaive over one shoulder and a horn lantern swinging in the other hand — you will see the lantern long before you see him, which is the whole point of him and your only advantage. He walks a round; if the lantern stops moving, he has heard something.

Silhouette. A warm glowing box at hip height, a broad-brimmed hat like an upturned bowl, and a pole rising 25 cm above his head — light, brim, pole, in that order.

The High Medieval · CurtainWall, InnerWard
Castle Crossbowmanranged
A hired marksman in mail coif and red padded jack, with a stirrup crossbow that takes an age to span.

A professional, which is to say a man paid by the bolt and careful with every one. He wears a mail coif under an iron skull cap, a red quilted jack in the household's colour, and carries a stirrup crossbow that will put a bolt through a door. It then takes him six long seconds, a foot in the stirrup and a belt hook, to span it again — which is when you run at him.

Silhouette. A grey rounded mail head on red shoulders, and the crossbow's wide horizontal prod across his hips — a T at waist height.

The High Medieval · Keep, InnerWard
Household Knightheavy
The lord's own knight in full mail, great helm and the household's arms — the one you go around.

And here, at last, is the gentleman the whole household is dressed to imitate: mail from crown to toe, a flat-topped great helm with a painted crest, the lord's arms on his surcoat and his shield. He is slow to wake and slower to turn, but he does not stop, and he does not care what you throw at him. Everything else in this castle can be outwitted; him, you avoid.

Silhouette. A flat-topped bucket head with a little fan on top, a long blue coat with a white chevron, and a big kite-like shield on the left — a rectangle, a chevron, a shield.

The High Medieval · OuterBailey, InnerWard
Alaunt War-houndspecial
A heavy-jawed fawn war-dog in a spiked collar and the household's padded coat, which hears you first.

I have been bitten by a great many things, and I tell you plainly that the alaunt is the worst of them: a broad-skulled hunting dog bred to hold a boar, wearing a spiked collar and a quilted coat in the lord's colours. It sleeps in the bailey and it wakes to noise — any noise — and it does not stop to think about it. It is faster than you, it knows the stairs, and it will have your ankle before the knight has found his helm.

Silhouette. A low, deep-chested dog shape with a blocky head held forward, a blue saddle-blanket shape on its back and a jagged ring of spikes at the neck.

The plunder

The High Medieval · one carrier · artifact
Arm Reliquary
A silver-gilt forearm raised in blessing, with a rock-crystal window onto a saint's bone.

Somebody's saint is in there, and somebody's lord paid a great deal to keep him in silver. A forearm and hand in chased silver-gilt, two fingers raised in blessing, standing on a stepped plinth, with a little oval of rock crystal through which you may inspect the relic — and through which, if you drop it, the whole enterprise will come apart. It is the second most valuable thing in the chapel and by far the easiest to carry off.

The High Medieval · one carrier
Silver Ewer
A hammered silver ewer with a long spout, hinged lid and the household's enamel medallion; it dents, it never breaks.

Two stone of silver that sits nicely under one arm and pours wine for the lord at table. It has a long elegant spout, a hinged lid with a gilt knob, a band of black niello, and a small enamel of the household arms in case anyone forgets whose it is. It will not break — silver does not break — but it dents, and every dent is a small, permanent confession.

Stratum III · c. 1450
c. 1450Stratum III
The Late Medieval

Plate, powder and suspicion

Fortresses within fortresses, built by men who had you specifically in mind. The gate turns a corner so you cannot run straight through it, the vault above it has seven holes and a man with a bucket of hot sand behind each, and the guards walk to a schedule written down by a Burgundian clerk who has never once been late. This is the first century in which the defenders own powder of their own, and the first in which they hunt in pairs — so when you hear one halberd scrape the flagstones, count to two.

The stonework

Three pieces of building. Each sits on the twelve-metre cell and knows its own joins.

The Late Medieval · CurtainWall
The Crooked Barbican
A gate passage that turns a right-angle under seven murder-holes, so nobody gets a straight run at the inner gate.

Whoever built this had met raiders before and did not care for them. You come in by the outer gate on the south face, walk north under four murder-holes, and then the passage turns east — deliberately, so you cannot see the inner gate, cannot run at it, and must spend a second or two wondering why the vault is ticking. Three more murder-holes wait along the second leg, keyhole gun-loops stare in from the guardroom, and every one of them was built for the new hand-cannon. It is a CurtainWall cell, open to the sky above the deck, and the only way into the castle that does not involve a ladder.

The Great Hall
The lord's hall: a raised dais and high table under a cloth of estate, an arch-braced roof, a hooded hearth and an 8-metre tapestry.

This is where the household eats, argues, and pretends not to be counting the silver. A high table on a dais under a crimson cloth of estate, a verdure tapestry eight metres long that cost more than the roof, a hooded hearth big enough to roast a disappointing guest, and an oak roof whose arch-braces meet so far above you that the candle wheel looks like a crown. It is full of things worth stealing and one thing worth burning, and the difficulty is telling the household which you meant.

The Counting House
The steward's office: a chequered counting table, four tiers of ledgers, a brick strong room behind an iron door and a strongbox sunk in the floor.

Where the Burgundian money actually lives, looked after by men who can tell a clipped coin by the sound it makes. A counting table under a chequered cloth, a balance, piles of coin laid out for the day; four tiers of ledgers that say who owes what (and, if you read carefully, who has been stealing); a brick strong room with an iron-latticed door and three locks; and — for those who look down — a strongbox sunk half a metre into the floor under a flagstone. Every lock here was fitted by someone paid by the lock.

The household

Four defenders: the one who walks the walls, the one who shoots, the one you avoid, and the one this century is remembered for.

The Late Medieval · CurtainWall, OuterBailey
Sallet Halberdierpatrol
The common guard of the Burgundian house: blackened sallet and bevor, brigandine under a saltire tabard, halberd at the slope — always walking with a partner.

The first thing to understand about this fellow is that there are two of him. Sallet and bevor, a brigandine studded with tinned rivets, a white livery tabard with the ragged red saltire of the house, and a halberd with a pierced blade and a nasty spike; he walks a round written in a book and he walks it with a partner ten paces behind. Knock one down and the other has already seen you do it. He is the patrol of the Late Medieval castle, on the walls and in the outer bailey, and he is the reason you learn to count footsteps.

Handgunnerranged
A quilted man in a kettle hat with a hand-gonne on an oak tiller and a lit slow match — slow to load, loud, and very bad news at twelve paces.

Here is the future, and it smells of rotten eggs. A padded linen jack, a steel kettle hat, a horn flask of powder and a pouch of lead, and on his shoulder a wrought-iron tube on an oak tiller that he fires by putting a glowing cord to a hole in it and hoping. He is slow — forty seconds to load, and the match gives him away in the dark — but when he fires, the whole ward hears it, and whatever he hits stays hit. He never works alone: find the pavise and you will find him behind it.

Twenty-five kilograms of the finest steel Augsburg can hammer, fluted like a cathedral and polished like a mirror, with a gentleman inside it who was raised from infancy for exactly this conversation. Armet with a sparrow-beak visor, cusped plackart, fan couters and poleyns, pointed sabatons, and a poleaxe with an axe, a four-pointed hammer and a spike, because he likes to have options. He is slow to wake and slow to turn, and your spells mostly slide off him. Do not fight him; do not be seen by him; if you must, make him walk through a door he is too proud to duck.

This is the Age's signature threat, and it is not a man so much as a partnership. The pavisier carries a great painted shield taller than your chest, plants it on its spiked feet with a prop behind it, and crouches there while his friend with the hand-gonne reloads in perfect safety. Separate him from his gunner and he is just a man with a very large board; leave them together and they will take the gate from you a pace at a time.

Every lord of consequence owns two harnesses: the one he fights in and the one he is seen in. This is the second — white steel, fluted, with bands of etched and gilded foliage running down the breast and round the sallet brow, strapped in crimson velvet with gilt buckles, and standing on its oak post in the corner of a chamber like a guest who will not leave. It is worth a great deal and weighs more than a man, so it needs two of you, a clear corridor, and no sudden ideas about stairs.

The Duke's household wears its wealth on its hats, and this one belonged to somebody who wanted to be noticed from across the hall. A gold quatrefoil no bigger than a thumb-joint, four white roses enamelled in the round, a table-cut balas ruby in four claws at the centre, seed pearls round the rim and a pearl drop swinging below. A nef is a ship made of money that sits in front of the lord at dinner to tell everyone which end of the table is his. This one is raised silver-gilt: a carrack with a crenellated sterncastle and forecastle, three masts, a fighting top with two tiny cast sailors, rigging of silver wire soldered at every stay, and a hinged lid in the deck under which the salt is kept. It is the finest thing on the Great Hall's high table, and the most delicate: the rigging will not survive being dropped, and the salt will go everywhere.

Stratum IV · c. 1620
c. 1620Stratum IV
The Age of Powder

Palaces, cabinets and gunpowder

Wide halls, enormous windows, glass by the acre — and, somewhere below the ballroom, a vaulted room full of black powder that turns any argument into demolition. This is an early-seventeenth-century Habsburg palace: lime-washed walls, black walnut, blued steel, and the richest, most delicate and most flammable plunder in the game, all under one roof. The household has learned from three centuries of you. It posts musketeers at the windows, sappers at the doors, and men in blackened plate in the cabinet rooms. One stray IGNIS near the magazine ends the evening, for them and for you.

The stonework

Three pieces of building. Each sits on the twelve-metre cell and knows its own joins.

The Age of Powder · Keep
The Long Gallery
An enfilade gallery of tall mullioned windows, mirrors between the piers, parquet underfoot — every surface in it is glass or wants to be.

The Long Gallery is where the family walks when it wishes to be seen walking: tall windows down one side, Venetian mirrors down the other, so that the light comes in twice and the thief is visible four times. It is a single Keep cell, laid on the north–south axis so that four of them in a row make the enfilade the architect was paid for. Parquet, portraits, a chandelier, and several thousand panes of forest glass — everything glass here shatters loudly, and the guards two rooms away hear it. Walk softly, carry nothing wider than the doorway, and do not cast anything bright.

The Powder Magazine
A vaulted brick chamber of barrels and kegs on racks, behind a copper-nailed door, lit only through glass from outside — the Age's hazard.

The magazine is the reason this palace can hold a siege, and the reason it may not survive one. Barrels of black powder stand on timber racks under a brick barrel-vault, the door is nailed with copper so nothing in the room can strike a spark, and the only light comes through a glazed lamp-box in the wall, fed from a passage outside. Everything in it is flammable; everything in it is, in a sense, a weapon. One stray IGNIS in here ends the evening: the whole cell detonates, and so do its neighbours.

A cabinet-of-curiosities room: glazed shelving cases, a stuffed crocodile hung from the ceiling, globes, and specimen jars by the hundred.

The Kunstkammer is the family's argument that it owns the whole world, arranged by size. Shelved cases line the walls from floor to cornice, glazed doors over coral, horn, shells and things in jars; two great globes stand on the floor like planets that have come down to be admired; and a stuffed crocodile hangs by chains from the ceiling, looking at you as though it has seen thieves before. Almost everything here is small, dear and breakable — the best plunder by weight in the palace, and the most delicate. Specimen jars are full of spirit, which burns.

The Palace Guard walks the terraces and the courts in the family's murrey livery, a morion on his head and a partisan on his shoulder, looking the way a palace wishes to look at night. He is mostly ornament, and he knows it, which makes him diligent. He walks a route, lifts his lantern to anything odd, and shouts before he strikes — the partisan's wide blade gives him reach through a doorway, and he will hold one alone rather than chase you into the dark. A cheap man to fool, and an expensive one to kill quietly.

A matchlock musketeer in a broad hat with a forked rest, a bandolier of twelve apostles and a lit match — slow, deafening, and wreathed in smoke.

The Musketeer is the household's argument at forty paces. He carries a matchlock taller than his shoulder and a forked rest to lay it on, a bandolier of twelve wooden powder chargers that click like teeth when he walks, and a slow match smouldering at both ends. He is slow — the volley takes him the better part of a minute to load — but it is heard across the palace, it fills the room with smoke, and it hits like a thrown door. His lit match is a travelling spark: keep him away from the magazine, or make sure he is near it and you are not.

Silhouette. A wide-brimmed felt hat with a plume over a buff coat, a long straight musket line (1.55 m) slanting over the shoulder, a forked stick in the other hand, and a ring of hanging bottles at chest height. Two tiny glowing points (the match ends) are the first thing you see in the dark.

The Age of Powder · Keep, InnerWard
Cuirassierheavy
A cuirassier dismounted into the cabinet rooms: blackened three-quarter armour, a closed burgonet, a brace of wheellock pistols and a heavy sword.

The Cuirassier is the last of the armoured men, a heavy horseman who has been told to walk the Kunstkammer at night and has been sulking about it for years. He is blackened plate from crown to knee, heavy and slow and very nearly bullet-proof, with a pair of wheellocks in his holsters — no burning match to warn you, two shots, and then the sword. He does not chase so much as arrive. Avoid him; if you cannot, make him turn, because the plate that saves his front has nothing to say about the backs of his knees.

Silhouette. A broad, dark, armoured column: a closed helmet with a peaked falling visor and a comb, huge layered shoulder-lames, a long skirt of steel tassets to the knee, and big soft leather boots below. Two pistol butts jut from the hip holsters like ball-ended antlers.

The Age of Powder · InnerWard, Keep
Petardierspecial
A sapper carrying a bell-shaped bronze petard bolted to a plank, and a belt of grenados — he blows doors, and himself, near magazines.

The Petardier is the household's locksmith for doors it does not have the key to. He carries a bronze petard — a bell of powder bolted to a heavy oak plank — which he hangs on any door you have barred, lights, and walks briskly away from; and a belt of grenados, which he throws after you when you run. He is an engineer and a coward in equal parts, which keeps him alive most nights. He is the Age's explosive special: his fuses are hazards to everyone, near a magazine he is a catastrophe, and the petard on his back goes off if you hit it with anything hot.

Silhouette. A short, stooped figure bowed under a big square plank on his back with a bell-shaped bronze pot fixed to it (mouth outward), a round leather cap, and a row of dark spheres on his belt. The plank and bell make a unique square-plus-dome hump at shoulder height.

The plunder

Five things worth the trip. Worth is coin at the lair; bulk is stone in your arms; the red bar is how little it takes to ruin it.

The Age of Powder · two carriers
Cabinet of Curiosities
An ebony Kunstschrank of forty drawers on a turned stand — two carriers, very dear, and it rains curios if you drop it.

The Kunstschrank is a whole Kunstkammer shrunk to a piece of furniture: ebony and walnut, forty little drawers, gilt mounts, painted panels, and in every drawer something rare enough to have been worth a ship. It is far too heavy for one thief and far too delicate for two — tilt it and the drawers slide, drop it and they burst open and scatter coral, cameos and small silver over the floor. It is the best haul in the Age that a crew can actually carry, and it will make them walk slowly.

Venetian Mirror
A large Venetian glass mirror in a walnut-and-gilt frame — two hands, extremely fragile, and it shows you the guard behind you.

Murano plate, tin-and-mercury silvered, in a walnut frame with a gilt inner moulding: a thing so valuable in 1620 that it cost more than the painting next to it. It is big, flat, two-handed and extremely fragile — the slightest knock and it goes in a sheet of shards and a sound heard two rooms off. While you carry it, it is also a mirror: you will see what is following you.

The Age of Powder · one carrier
Astrolabe
A gilt-brass planispheric astrolabe with rete, plates and alidade — sturdy, and it dents before it breaks.

An astrolabe is the sky in your hand — a brass disc engraved with the stars, a pierced rete that turns over it, and a sighting rule on the back — and this one was gilt by a Nuremberg maker so that it would look as expensive as it was. It is one-handed, dense, and sturdy; you can drop it and it will only dent. Hit it hard enough and the rete snaps loose, and then it is only a very handsome plate.

Silver Service Tureen
A silver tureen with a domed lid and a ladle — the lid pops off at the slightest excuse.

The tureen is the centrepiece of the silver service, an oval pot of hammered silver on four lion's feet with a domed lid and a ladle that sticks out of a notch like a flag. It is a respectable haul, a comfortable two-hand carry, and treacherous in one respect: the lid pops off at any jolt, clangs on the floor, and rolls away making the noise of a small bell. Hold the lid, or leave it.

Nautilus Cup
A pearly nautilus shell in a silver-gilt mount on a sea-monster stem — the most valuable, most fragile thing in the palace.

The Nautilus Cup is the Age's crown jewel: a real shell from the far side of the world, stripped to its pearl, mounted in silver-gilt on a stem of a triton riding a sea-monster, and never once drunk from. It is small, light, and so fragile that sneezing near it is a gamble. It is also the most valuable thing in the palace, and the family will know within the hour that it has gone.
